key: The cremasteric reflex and the clock decide it: torsion is an abrupt vascular emergency with an absent reflex, a high horizontal testis and absent Doppler flow, whereas epididymitis is gradual infection with a present reflex, relief on lifting and increased flow.
items: A twisted cord cuts off venous outflow within moments, so severe pain arrives suddenly instead of building over days as infection does.
Torsion abolishes the reflex in nearly every case, whereas infection leaves it intact, making it the best single bedside discriminator.
High-riding testis with a horizontal lie
Twisting shortens the cord and rotates the testis, lifting it and turning it sideways, while an infected epididymis leaves the lie normal.
Sudden severe pain from an ischemic organ triggers autonomic symptoms, whereas epididymitis tends to cause local pain with urinary symptoms.
Absent or reduced flow on Doppler
Venous and then arterial inflow are blocked by the twist, while inflamed tissue shows increased flow.
A tunica vaginalis attached too high lets the testis hang free and twist on its cord, and the defect is usually bilateral.
Torsion peaks in adolescence, with a smaller peak in newborns, whereas epididymitis affects sexually active men and older men with urinary obstruction.
Infection ascends from the urethra or bladder and inflames the epididymis progressively, so symptoms evolve over days rather than minutes.
The cord is not twisted, so the reflex arc is intact and stroking the inner thigh still lifts the testis.
Lifting the testis eases the pain (Prehn sign)
Elevation relieves tension on an inflamed epididymis, but a twisted cord gains no relief, although the sign is unreliable and must not delay surgery.
Ascending infection from the urethra or bladder leaves signs of urinary tract inflammation, which are absent in torsion.
Inflammation raises perfusion of the epididymis and testis, the opposite of the reduced flow caused by torsion.
Chlamydia or gonorrhea in a man younger than 35
These sexually transmitted organisms are the usual cause in younger men, whereas enteric rods dominate in older men.
Treated with antibiotics rather than emergency surgery
Infection responds to antibiotics chosen for the likely organism, while a twisted cord needs surgery within hours.
